slides.text:
**AI agents just rediscovered telegraphese.**

One instruction gets models writing in 1866-style telegraph shorthand.

The trick cuts their output tokens by up to 49%.

Writer Travis Smith ran a benchmark he calls the Telegraph Test.

He told several models to answer in terse, cablese-style records.

Other models, never shown an example, read those records back at full accuracy.

This is an old problem: compressing language when every word is metered.

SMS and early Twitter forced the same shorthand culture, decades later.

The compressed style isn't something anyone had to invent.

It's already baked into training data, from telegrams to text messages.

That's why models write fluent cablese cold, with zero examples.
The savings only show up if you compress in the right spot.
bullets: Use it in scratchpads and handoffs.
Expand it back for human readers.

slides.text: Not everyone in the discussion was convinced this is new.

panel.big: "Just AI slop dressed up as caveman-speak."

slides.text:
**My rule: compress for the model, not the person.**

Output tokens cost three to five times more than input tokens.

That tax disappears the moment the reader is another model.

Where have you had to write for an audience that wasn't really reading?

**Tell me in the comments,** and save this before your next agent run.
